You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 Drafting Review: Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Enforcement Gaps

These issues are based on the manager's amendment text as pasted. For coverage, the safest framing is "questions the text leaves open." Some have plausible answers in existing law or legislative history, and sponsors or committee counsel may have responses.

## Sec. 2: Definitions

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A): Per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton cap applies "by a single vessel," so an operator could spread recovery across several vessels, each under the cap, with no limit on total output. There is no aggregation rule by operator, project, or corporate family.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A): Undefined measurement.** The text doesn't say whether tons are wet or dry weight. Freshly recovered nodules hold a lot of water, so the choice materially changes the effective cap. "Per year" is also undefined: calendar year, fiscal year, or any rolling 12 months.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "Recovery" undefined.** It's unclear whether recovery means lifting material to the surface, or also includes collecting, crushing, or relocating it on the seabed. Activities that cause seabed disturbance without bringing material aboard a vessel may fall outside the definition.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A): "From the seabed" and the vessel requirement.** "From the seabed" could be read to exclude resources in the subsoil, such as sulfide deposits that require cutting below the surface. Recovery to a fixed platform, or by a collector system not counted as "a vessel," may also escape.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A): 200-meter depth line.** The text doesn't say how depth is measured: at the point of extraction, the water depth of the site, or the deepest point. Operations straddling the line create disputes.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B): "The Secretary" is never identified.** The Act doesn't say which Secretary (Commerce? Interior?). This creates an immediate authority question and a litigation hook for any determination made under this clause.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B): Open-ended delegation with criminal consequences.** An agency determination of "comparable" risk can make conduct a crime under Sec. 5(b). Yet the clause has no standard, rulemaking procedure, notice requirement, or definition of "comparable." That invites vagueness and nondelegation challenges and could leave determinations unenforceable.

8. **Sec. 2(2): Entity types left out.** "Corporation" arguably excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and other entity forms commonly used for project vehicles.

9. **Sec. 2(2): "State" undefined.** Without a definition, it's unclear whether entities organized in DC, Puerto Rico, or other territories, or federally chartered entities, are covered.

10. **Sec. 2(2): Foreign subsidiaries and residents excluded.** A U.S. company's foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not a "U.S. person," so the extraterritorial reach in Sec. 3(a) can be avoided by mining through an offshore affiliate. Lawful permanent residents are also excluded.

11. **Sec. 2(3): Covered vessel is disconnected from the prohibition.** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold applies only to the registry. Smaller vessels can mine without registering, and nothing ties registry data to enforcing the tonnage cap.

12. **Sec. 2(3): "Equipped for" is ambiguous.** It's unclear whether a vessel is covered only while equipment is installed, or whether removable or modular equipment counts. Operators could arguably install systems after registration deadlines or swap them between vessels. The tonnage measurement standard is also unspecified.

13. **Sec. 2 generally: Key terms undefined.** "Person," "mineral resources," "exploration license," "environmental assessment," "serious harm," and "operator" are all undefined, though each is load-bearing elsewhere in the Act.

## Sec. 3: Prohibition

14. **Sec. 3(a): Geographic scope unclear.** "In the United States" doesn't say whether it includes the territorial sea, the EEZ, or the outer continental shelf. That matters for foreign persons operating in U.S. waters.

15. **Sec. 3(a): Only extraction is prohibited.** The text does not reach financing, sponsoring, chartering vessels to, purchasing, importing, processing, or selling resources mined by non-U.S. persons. U.S. firms could stay in the supply chain while a foreign partner does the recovery.

16. **Sec. 3(a): No anti-evasion provision.** There is no clause covering structuring, causing, or conspiring to cause a violation. General federal conspiracy and aiding-and-abetting statutes would reach some criminal conduct but not civil liability.

17. **Sec. 3(b): Grandfather clause permits "mining" under an exploration license.** Exploration licenses (e.g., under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act) generally don't authorize commercial recovery. The clause either exempts nothing, or it can be read to bless commercial-scale "mining" by anyone holding an older exploration license. Either reading invites litigation.

18. **Sec. 3(b): Issuing authority unspecified.** The text doesn't say whether this means only U.S. (NOAA) licenses, or also exploration contracts issued by the International Seabed Authority or foreign sponsoring states. A broad reading would exempt many existing international contractors' partners.

19. **Sec. 3(b): No limits on the grandfathered license.** Nothing addresses renewals, extensions, amendments, transfers, or expansion of licensed areas. A pre-enactment license could arguably support activity indefinitely and could be sold to new operators.

20. **Sec. 3(b): Cutoff tied to enactment, not the effective date.** Licenses issued during the 180-day window between enactment and the effective date (Sec. 8) are not grandfathered. Applications pending at enactment are not addressed, which creates a potential reliance or takings argument for applicants.

21. **Sec. 3(c): The environmental-assessment exemption has no limits.** It has no tonnage cap, permit, approval, oversight, or definition. Because purpose is self-declared, commercial-scale "pilot" or "test" mining could be labeled assessment. There is no rule against selling material recovered under the exemption.

22. **Sec. 3 generally: Relationship to existing law unaddressed.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or reconcile with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, which authorizes NOAA to issue commercial recovery permits. Operators holding or seeking DSHMRA permits will argue that the two statutes conflict.

## Sec. 4: Registry

23. **Sec. 4: No penalties for registry violations.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing inaccurate reports carries no specific penalty. The general false-statements statute (18 U.S.C. 1001) may apply to knowingly false certifications.

24. **Sec. 4(a): No deadline or jurisdictional hook.** The text sets no time to register and doesn't say whether it applies only to U.S.-flagged vessels, U.S. operators, or any vessel operating in U.S. waters.

25. **Sec. 4(b): No required report contents.** Reports need not include tonnage (wet or dry), location, depth, dates, or buyers, which is exactly the information needed to test the Sec. 2(1)(A) threshold.

26. **Sec. 4(b): Self-certification only.** The text provides no independent monitoring (vessel tracking, observers, inspections, audits) and no recordkeeping or record-retention requirement. Unregistered vessels never file reports at all.

27. **Sec. 4: No rulemaking authority.** NOAA isn't given authority to issue regulations implementing the registry, and there is no funding authorization.

## Sec. 5: Penalties

28. **Sec. 5: No enforcement agency or procedure.** The text doesn't say who assesses civil penalties, what notice and hearing are required, or how judicial review works. It also provides no investigative, boarding, subpoena, seizure, or forfeiture authority, which weakens practical enforcement.

29. **Sec. 5(a): Per-day penalty vs. per-year definition.** The violation is defined by annual tonnage, but the penalty runs per day. It's unclear when a violation "occurs" (only once the 10,000th ton is recovered, or every day of that year's operations), which complicates penalty calculation.

30. **Sec. 5(a): Penalty date conflicts with the effective date.** The text applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but under Sec. 8 the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Conduct in the window is either not a violation, making the clause confusing, or is penalized retroactively, raising due process concerns and ex post facto concerns for Sec. 5(b).

31. **Sec. 5(b): Criminal liability resting on vague terms.** A 10-year felony depending on undefined terms and an unspecified Secretary's "comparable risk" determinations (Items 6–7, 13) is vulnerable to vagueness challenges, at least as applied to Sec. 2(1)(B) activities.

32. **Sec. 5: No citizen suit or private enforcement.** Enforcement depends entirely on executive-branch priorities.

## Sec. 6: International Agreement

33. **Sec. 6: Ambiguous deadline.** "Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" could mean start negotiating or conclude an agreement within 18 months. Either way, "seek to" is not binding. There's no reporting requirement to Congress and no consequence if nothing happens.

34. **Sec. 6: "Equivalent" undefined, and a forum issue.** It's unclear whether an agreement must match the tonnage threshold, the exemptions, or the extraterritorial reach. The text also doesn't address how this fits with the International Seabed Authority process, given that the U.S. is not a party to UNCLOS.

## Sec. 7: Duration

35. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b): Internal conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition stays in effect *until* Congress acts, while (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. A court must decide which controls, though (b) likely wins as the more specific provision.

36. **Sec. 7(b): The sunset lets operators wait it out.** The sunset ends the prohibition, the registry, and the penalties together. Operators holding claims or licenses can simply wait 10 years. It's also unclear whether pending enforcement actions survive the sunset, since there is no savings clause.

37. **Sec. 7(a): The NASEM-and-joint-resolution mechanism is largely hollow.** No NASEM study is commissioned, funded, or scheduled. A joint resolution signed by the President is simply a new law, which Congress could pass anyway. "Serious harm" is undefined, and the clause doesn't say what happens after such a finding (does the prohibition end automatically?).

## Sec. 8: Effective Date

38. **Sec. 8: 180-day lead time.** The delay opens a window for operators to begin or accelerate recovery, restructure into non-U.S. entities, or move vessels before the prohibition applies. It also interacts awkwardly with Sec. 3(b) and Sec. 5(a) (Items 20, 30).

## Omissions Across the Bill

39. **No severability clause.** If one provision is struck down (e.g., Sec. 2(1)(B) on delegation grounds), there's no express direction that the rest survives.

40. **No authorization of appropriations.** The registry, enforcement, State Department negotiations, and any NASEM study have no funding authorization.

**Sourcing note:** I've worked only from the text you pasted. Before publishing any of these points, please confirm them against the official manager's amendment text on Congress.gov or from committee staff. It would also be worth asking the sponsors' offices about Items 17, 22, 30, and 35, since those are the most consequential and the most likely to have an explanation or a planned fix at markup.
